subject: literature
passage: Pyotr Ilyich Krasnov read his son's letter standing, as he read invoices, and when he had finished he laid it on the counting-house desk beside the ledger and observed to his clerk that the boy wrote a fair hand. The letter announced that Alexei had left the university at Moscow, had taken employment with a newspaper of which his father had never heard, and was, he wrote, happier than he had been in three years. Krasnov said nothing further about it that day. But the clerk, who had served him for twenty years, noticed that the old man twice entered the same shipment of hemp in the ledger, and that on the second occasion he did not notice his error at all, but sat for some time afterward with the pen lifted, looking not at the page but at the window.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: A merchant angrily refuses to discuss his son's news with his longtime clerk.
choices.B: A merchant shows that his accounts matter more to him than his son's future.
choices.C: A merchant is quietly proud that his son has found work that makes him truly happy.
choices.D: A merchant's businesslike calm hides a disturbance that surfaces in his work.

explanation.why: Two parts of the text must be read together. At first Krasnov treats the letter like an invoice, commenting only on the handwriting and saying "nothing further." But the clerk sees him enter the same shipment twice, miss the error, and stare at the window. The contrast shows that the news has unsettled him beneath his composed surface. The text does not say exactly what he feels, so the key names a disturbance without specifying it.
explanation.A: Incorrect. He says nothing more about the letter, but the text shows no anger and no refusal.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This reverses the clue: his mistakes in the ledger show that the letter has pushed his accounts out of his mind.
explanation.C: Incorrect. His only comment is on the handwriting, and his later distraction suggests unease; nothing in the text shows pride.
explanation.D: Correct. His calm, invoice-like handling of the letter contrasts with the uncharacteristic errors and distraction the clerk observes.
